sections.heading: Where the Hills Meet the Highlands
sections.body: Somewhere between Huntly and Raglan, where the Waikato land folds itself into steep green hills and soft, wet hollows, you'll find Waikato Highlands. This is not flat, easy country. It rolls and rises, holds water in its gullies long after the rain has passed, and asks a lot of anything that tries to live on it. It is beautiful, stubborn land — and it needed an animal just as beautiful and just as stubborn to belong here.

sections.heading: Why Highlands
sections.body: There is something almost inevitable about Highland cattle on ground like ours. These are animals bred for centuries in the wet, wind-scoured glens of Scotland — built low and dense and shaggy, sure-footed on slopes that would defeat softer breeds, content to graze wetland margins that other cattle simply avoid. When we looked at our hills and our boggy corners and asked what belonged here, the answer wasn't something we had to force. It was already written into the breed's blood.

But it isn't only practicality that drew us in, if we're honest. There is real emotion in these animals. Anyone who has stood in a paddock with a Highland cow — that great sweep of horn, that impossibly soft, wind-blown fringe of hair falling over dark, patient eyes — knows they are not just livestock. They carry an old-world dignity with them, a calm and a character that is genuinely rare. They are gentle with their calves, steady in temperament, and they seem to know, in some quiet animal way, that they are exactly where they are supposed to be.
